info.name: Cartoon fact short
info.tagline: A fast, flat narrator walks through a cause-and-effect chain while the camera keeps moving between still 3D tableaux.
info.description: Shorts of about 29 s in 9:16. A deadpan voice at about 196 wpm opens on the consequence with a concrete number, then chains cause to effect and stops on the outcome. Sets and figures stay frozen like dioramas. The camera makes one move per shot and a new picture arrives about every 1.9 s. Every fact gets its own literal close-up, and numbers sit on glowing in-world displays. The only overlay is a small white caption.
story: Opens on the consequence or action already happening, with a concrete count, in one sentence of 11–14 words. No questions.
Chains steps with so / while / until / as / which / minutes later, one blunt physical verb per step.
Uses 3–5 sentences and about 80–90 words, ending on the outcome word. No outro, moral or call to action.
Pairs any unfamiliar mechanism with one everyday object it works like.
Keeps the narration deadpan, with no opinions or jokes, and leaves the longest pause (about 0.6 s) before the payoff.
look: Clean semi-real 3D with no outlines or toon shading, plausible materials and one clear key light.
A limited palette per scene. The saturated accent goes only to the key object or the protagonists.
Figures are frozen stand-ins about 7 heads tall with small, fixed faces. Pose does the acting.
The camera is the performer: one move per shot on one axis, never reversed, with at most one hold.
Numbers sit on glowing in-world displays. The only overlay is a small white caption at 78% of frame height, in 2–4 word chunks.

ideas.label: The canal jam
ideas.idea: A single cargo ship turns sideways in a narrow canal and stops hundreds of other ships for six days. Show how one gust and one wrong angle backed up a whole trade route.

ideas.label: How a lighthouse reaches the horizon
ideas.idea: An explainer on how a lamp no brighter than a few household bulbs is seen 20 miles out at sea: the ring lens, the rotation and the flash pattern that tells each lighthouse apart.

ideas.label: The beehive air conditioner
ideas.idea: On a hot day, thousands of bees keep their hive at 35 °C. Show the water carriers, the fanning lines at the entrance and the evaporation that cools the combs.

stages.series:
This series uses the "Cartoon fact short" template.
- Each episode is one roughly 29 s fact or true story built as a physical chain of cause and effect, where every step can be shown as a literal picture.
- Two kinds fit. True story (third person, past tense): a threat, a small unrelated action, what it caused, the threat striking, the payoff. Process explainer (second person, present tense, the viewer as the object): how something works, step by step.
- Every episode needs a concrete number for the hook (a count, a time, a distance or a temperature) and an outcome it can end on.
- If the idea names one story, split it into episodes at natural cause-and-effect breaks (what led up to it, the event, what it changed). If the idea names a theme, give each episode its own story.
- Stick to well-documented facts. Each synopsis states the number, the chain in one line and the outcome. No jokes and no morals.
stages.series_extend: Keep the "Cartoon fact short" formula: one visual chain of cause and effect per episode, hooked on a concrete number and ending on the outcome. Alternate true stories and process explainers where the theme allows. Don't repeat a story, mechanism or hook number already used.
stages.bible:
This series uses the "Cartoon fact short" template, which always builds its own world: return an empty `cast`.
- `style.palette`: a limited set with one hot accent kept for the key object, e.g. slate #5b5f66, near-black #121315, sky blue #4a7fb8, pale haze #c7d6e2, hot orange #ff6a1f, with a cool glow colour #1fb5c9 for glowing displays. Use darker, muted values for danger and true stories, and brighter, complementary ones for explainers.
- `style.mood`: deadpan, documentary, precise, relentless.
- `style.captionStyle`: small white bold sans, centred low (about 78% of frame height), 2–4 words, no box, no emphasis colour.
- `style.grade`: the kit grade closest to a clean, neutral, crisp render ("none" if nothing fits). Never film grain or a stylised cartoon grade.
stages.world:
House style for this series ("Cartoon fact short"). It overrides the general look advice where they differ.

Characters are semi-real stand-ins, not cartoons:
- Realistic proportions: about 7 head-heights tall, legs about half the body, limbs `capsule`s at natural thickness, a slightly oval `sphere` head.
- Faces are tiny and fixed: two small dark eyes, no mouth tube or only a faint one, `blinks: false`. Never give cartoon eyes or mouths to objects or creatures.
- Build one person model and reuse it. Dress it in one outfit in one bright accent colour (e.g. #ff6a1f or #f2c14e) so it reads as the same person in every shot. Background crowd copies wear muted greys and browns.
- Materials are plausible: skin and cloth `rough` 0.6–0.8, metal and glass low rough for crisp highlights.

Locations are clean dioramas with one obvious subject:
- Each location is one readable place with no stray props. Build a dense, full-scale place for scale shots and a sparse surface for close work.
- Put every number on an in-world display prop: a flat panel or box with a bright self-lit-looking material (a cool glow colour #1fb5c9 or white) large enough to fill 60–70% of the width in a close shot.
- When the story has a hidden or internal process, add a cutaway location: a frame-filling cross-section of the inside.
- Add one hinge location: the key object alone on near-black (ground and sky #0b0b0c, no fog colour showing), lit by one overhead key.
- Danger or true-story exteriors: overcast and flat. Sky top #5a6370, middle #7c858f, horizon #9aa2aa, sun elevation 50–70, sunColour #e6e9ec, sunStrength 1.5–2, fill 1.4–1.8, grey fog at density 0.01–0.02 so the threat looks hazy.
- Explainer or bright exteriors: sky top #4a7fb8, middle #8fb0cf, horizon #c7d6e2, sun azimuth 40–70, elevation 45–60, sunColour #fff4e2, sunStrength 3–3.5, fill 1.0–1.3, fog the horizon colour at 0.004–0.008.
- Interiors: near-black surroundings (#121315) with one overhead pool of light on the subject. Keep fill low (0.3–0.6) so the edges fall dark.
- Keep the ground behind the lower part of frame mid-to-dark and low in detail, because captions sit there.
- Marks: one mark per subject with the subject centred. Add one wide mark per location that can open and close an episode from the same angle. Keep 2 m clear in front of every mark.
stages.script:
This episode uses the "Cartoon fact short" formula. Write about 80–90 words in 3–5 sentences, for about 29 s at 196 wpm.
1. Hook: one declarative sentence of 11–14 words with the subject or threat already in action and a concrete count. It must end by about 4.7 s. Never a question or 'did you know'.
2. Setup and escalation: the longest sentence, steps chained with so / while / until / as / which / minutes later and -ing result clauses, one blunt physical verb per step.
3. The turn: start it with 'But' (use 'But' only here and in the payoff).
4. Outcome: end on its key word. Where possible, repeat the word that ends the hook. In a process piece, end on the final physical action, with the last sentence starting 'Then'.
- For a true story, use 5 beats of about 11/28/16/19/14 words. For an explainer, use 3 sentences of about 14/40/26 words.
- If a mechanism is unfamiliar, add one line comparing it to an everyday object (at most 2 per episode).
- Use plain words only: no opinions, jokes, morals, outro or call to action. Say what the picture can't (how much, why).
- Delivery: `neutral` on almost every line, intensity 0.35–0.45. Raise to 0.6 on the hook and on the line with the twist or impact verb (`tense` for danger, otherwise neutral). Never `warm` or `grieving`. Lift pitch for emphasis, never slow down.
- Pauses: 300–400 ms after a sentence, 0 ms inside a clause, about 600 ms before the payoff sentence, and 0 ms after the last line.
stages.shots:
This episode uses the "Cartoon fact short" template.
- Change picture about every 1.9 s, carrying about 4 words (range 2–6.5). Never run the whole episode at one shot length. Alternate quick shots of 1–1.6 s with result or explanation shots of 3–4.8 s (10–14 words).
- The first shot starts on word 1 and shows the subject or threat already acting. The first cut comes at about 1.7 s (0.9–2.5 s), on the word naming who or what is affected.
- Start shots mid-sentence, never on the first word after a sentence end. Put `fromWord` on or just before the noun the shot shows.
- Every fact, time or rule gets its own close-up of the thing doing it. Numbers go to the display location. Hidden processes go to the cutaway location. A comparison gets a shot of the everyday object.
- When a line lists or counts parts, cut a burst of 4–6 short inserts of 6–12 frames each, about 1 word apiece, one per part.
- Give the turning point one short shot (about 1.1 s) on the hinge location: the key object alone on black. Allow only one near-still shot per episode.
- Claims about many people show two or three recurring figures doing the action inside a crowd.
- The last shot is a wide at the opening location and angle, so the episode loops.
- cameraHint: one move per shot. Push-in by default, otherwise one pan or tilt. Pull back on the last shot.
stages.scene:
House style ("Cartoon fact short"):
- Camera: one continuous move per shot on one axis, never reversed. Default is push_in, otherwise tracking (pan or tilt). Shake is always 0. Cruise at about 23.5 %/s. Short inserts creep at 5–8 %/s. A big establishing or threat shot gets one steady 40–50% zoom over 3–4 s.
- Enter each shot fast (about 2.4× cruise) and ease down to cruise over 6–18 frames. Speed up again to about 1.2× in the last 8–15 frames so the shot leaves moving.
- The single hinge shot is near-still. In its last 10 frames, ease up to about 50 %/s.
- Use focus_on as a reveal: go from soft to sharp over about 10 frames and finish 3–6 frames before the subject is named.
- The final shot uses pull_back and slows to almost zero on the last word. Never end on a fast move.
- Rigs: low_hero for scale or the threat, high_down for crowds and aftermath, close for inserts and displays. Keep the subject in the centre column.
- Actors are frozen between beats: no idle actions or drift. Each action is a quick hit of about 4 frames, starting 1–5 frames before its word, about 7 per 10 s. Start repeated loops (pumping, pulsing) 10–12 frames before the verb. Allow at most one longer climax action (9–11 frames, then hold).
- Expressions stay neutral and never change. Emotion comes from one pose per figure per shot: slumped, upright or crouched. When an action carries into the following shot, open already in the key pose.
- Display values change instantly, about 10 frames after the number is spoken.
- Captions: 2–4 words per chunk with punctuation removed. Each chunk appears within ±3 frames of its first word. Hold one chunk across fast inserts and through pauses. No emphasis styling.
stages.publish: House style ("Cartoon fact short"): name the video with the fact and its number, flat and declarative ("How one stuck ship stopped 400 others"). No question openers and no hype words. The description is one plain line with the place, the year (or the process named) and the source. Use 3–5 hashtags on the topic plus #facts and #shorts.
